name: Mark Zuckerberg
title: The Kid Who Kept Saying No
subtitle: From a Risk game coded in sixth grade to a Harvard dorm room and total control of Meta: how Mark Zuckerberg builds, refuses to sell, and sometimes gets it badly wrong.
hook: As a high-school senior at Phillips Exeter Academy, Mark Zuckerberg and his friend Adam D'Angelo built a free music player called Synapse that learned what you liked to hear. After the tech site Slashdot wrote about it in April 2003, one company offered them ==$950,000==, on one condition: work for it for three years. His answer: "We wanted to go to college, so we said no." When the pair later changed their minds, the buyer had lost interest. Less than a year after that refusal, on ==4 February 2004==, he launched thefacebook.com from his Harvard dorm.

contact.howToReach: There is no public personal email for Mark Zuckerberg, and nothing you send to Meta's switchboard or inboxes will be passed to him just because you asked. chapters.title: The Boy Above the Dentist's Office

blocks.text: Mark Zuckerberg was born in ==1984== in White Plains, New York. He grew up nearby in Dobbs Ferry, a small village in Westchester County, New York. He was the second of four children and the only boy.

His father, Edward, was a dentist. His mother, Karen Kempner, trained as a psychiatrist. The two met on a blind date while they were students in New York: Edward was studying dentistry at NYU and Karen was at Brooklyn College. They married in 1979 and moved to Dobbs Ferry in 1980.

The four children arrived over five years. Randi was born in 1982, Mark in 1984, Donna in 1985 and Arielle in 1987. Randi later worked at Facebook as a marketing head, Donna became a classics scholar, and Arielle became a venture capitalist.
Four kids. One house. And the family business was downstairs.
A dental clinic on the ground floor

Here is the detail that explains a lot. Edward did not commute to an office. He ran his dental practice from the ground floor of the family home, and Karen handled the business side of it. Patients came and went below while the kids grew up above.
I had the unique situation of practicing in my house.

His practice was called Painless Dr. Z, and its slogan was =="We cater to cowards."== Edward later wrote that he and Karen developed ways to treat patients who were scared of the dentist, and that Karen's psychiatry training shaped how he worked. A clinic built around nervous patients is, at heart, a business about understanding people.

Edward also loved gadgets. He started computerizing his office in the mid-1980s, around the time Mark was born. "My kids all grew up around the office and were all exposed to computers," he told a Westchester radio station in 2011.

For example: the family's early Atari 800 home computer "came with a disk for programming," Edward recalled. Mark also had a book on programming, but his father says that, in the end, Mark's skill was self-taught.

photo.caption: An Atari 800, the kind of home computer Edward Zuckerberg says came with a programming disk. This is where the Zuckerberg kids first met code.
photo.author: Evan-Amos

blocks.text: A computer of his own

Mark got his own computer young. His father puts it at about age 8 or 9, around the same time his older sister Randi got one. Mark himself told the Harvard Crimson he started programming when he got his first computer in sixth grade. TIME reported that he began coding on a Quantex 486DX running Windows 3.1.

The kids' computers and the clinic shared one internet line, so they competed for it. The office needed the connection for insurance claims, so the children had only half an hour online before office hours ended at 5 p.m. In 1996 Edward fixed it the expensive way: he wired the whole house and brought in a T-1 line, a fast business connection that he says cost about ==$150 to $200 a month==.
A dad who paid for fast internet in 1996. That's a head start.

By about 12, his father says, Mark had full-time internet access and could talk to the other computers in the house. Randi, about two and a half years older, had been given a computer at around the same time as Mark. Edward's view was simple: "There are advantages to being exposed to computers early on."
ZuckNet: the first network he built

Around age 12, Mark built a home network he called ZuckNet. It let the computers in the house and in the dental office send messages to each other. A professional did the physical wiring; Mark wrote the software that made the machines talk.

For example: instead of shouting across the house, the front desk could send a message that a patient had arrived, and the hygienist could ping that a room was ready. Edward says the office used ZuckNet this way in 1996.

Edward likes to call ZuckNet =="the world's first social media network, theoretically."== That is a proud father talking, not a historian. But the real point is simpler. __Mark's first program was not a game or a homework tool. It was a way for people in one building to talk to each other.__
He learned the meaning of people being social and interacting with each other at a very early age.
What he was like at 5 and at 10
Ask his father what young Mark was like and you get two words: =="strong-willed and relentless."== Edward added a line that every parent of a stubborn kid will recognise.
For Mark, if he asked for something, yes by itself would work, but no required much more.

That stubbornness came with a playful streak. Mark and his older sister Randi liked pranks and home-made movies, as the next chapter shows. His father described him as a good student with "a special affinity for math and sciences," and as humble and quiet.
Strong-willed and quiet. Not the loud kid. The relentless one.

Edward's own parenting rule was not to push his children down one path. He told callers on that 2011 radio show that the job of a parent is "to recognize what their strengths are and support their strengths," with a balance of work and play. For Mark, the strength was obvious early: computers.

It also mattered that the family had money and time to spare. Years later Mark said so himself. "My parents worked really hard to make sure me and my sisters could go to good schools," he told People magazine.

blocks.text: So by 12, the pattern was already set. A boy who lived above a busy clinic, surrounded by computers his father paid for, had written software whose whole purpose was to connect people. He did not yet know that this was a business. He just thought it was fun.

There is an honest lesson here for any young reader. Mark's start was not a rags-to-riches story. He had two professional parents, a computer at home before most kids, and a father who treated technology as part of the family business. __Talent mattered, but so did access. If you lack the access, the fix is to find it: a library, a school lab, a friend's machine, a free online course.__
Lesson: notice what you build for fun. It's often your real talent.

chapters.title: Games, Latin and a Music Robot

blocks.text: At 13, Mark had a Star Wars-themed bar mitzvah. It fits. His teenage years were a mix of science fiction, video games and building things on his computer late into the night.

He and his sister Randi made their own movies. One winter break they filmed a home-made Star Wars parody they called ==The Star Wars Sill-ogy==. Their younger sister played the robot R2-D2. "We took our job very seriously," Randi told TIME.

For example: on New Year's Eve 1999, when many adults feared the "Y2K bug" would crash computers at midnight, Mark, then 15, and Randi switched off the house's power right at midnight. Their parents were worried about exactly that.
Fifteen, and already pranking adults about computers crashing.
Some kids played games. Mark wrote them.

Mark's real hobby was writing his own games. He wrote a computer version of Monopoly set at his middle school. He also wrote a version of the board game Risk set in the ancient Roman Empire, which he later called the first serious program he ever designed.
You played against Julius Caesar. He was good, and I was never able to win.

How did he learn? His first formal lesson came from a book, ==C++ For Dummies==. But he told the Crimson that most of what he knew came from friends. __He learned by building things he wanted to use, and by asking people who knew more.__
No bootcamp. One 'Dummies' book and friends. Start with what you have.
He also had heroes. One childhood hero was Justin Frankel, the programmer who created the Winamp music player. Keep that name in mind. Mark's first famous project would be built as a Winamp plug-in.
Outgrowing the local school
Mark went to Ardsley High School, the public school near home, until his junior year. He felt it was too small for what he wanted to learn.
[Ardsley] didn't have a lot of computer courses or a lot of the higher math courses.

So at about 16 he transferred to Phillips Exeter Academy, an old and famous boarding school in New Hampshire. Here is the surprise. He did not pick Exeter for its computers. ==Its biggest selling point for him was the Latin program.== He even planned to study classics, the languages and history of ancient Greece and Rome, at Harvard before he changed course.

photo.caption: The Academy Building at Phillips Exeter Academy in New Hampshire. Mark transferred here for his last two years of school, drawn by its Latin program.
photo.author: Transmarinus at English Wikipedia

blocks.text: At Exeter he stood out for two things that have nothing to do with code: ancient languages and fencing. The love of Rome stuck. Remember, his first big game was set in the Roman Empire, and he played against Caesar.
A coder who chose a school for Latin. Interests can mix.

The move itself is worth noticing. At 16, Mark decided his school was holding him back and left home for a tougher one. __When your environment runs out of things to teach you, changing it is a real decision, not a failure.__
Synapse: the music player that learned your taste

In his senior year at Exeter, Mark did an independent project with a classmate, Adam D'Angelo. Together they built ==Synapse==, a music player that watched what you listened to and learned your taste. Then it built playlists of songs you were likely to enjoy. They gave it away free as a plug-in for Winamp, the player made by Mark's hero.

For example: you play a few songs you love, the software spots the pattern, and it lines up similar tracks for you. Two teenagers at a boarding school built that idea around 2002, using machine learning.

In April 2003 the tech news site Slashdot posted about the project under the headline "Machine Learning and MP3s." Big companies noticed. TIME reported that AOL and Microsoft both tried to buy Synapse for around ==$1 million==. The Crimson reported that Winamp was interested too, and that a second offer reached about $2 million.
Some companies offered us right off the bat up to one million.
Taking the deal would have meant skipping college to keep working on the product. Mark and Adam said no. Mark chose Harvard instead.

Then came a twist. After they started college, the two decided they would sell after all. But by then the buyer had lost interest, and the deal was gone. __A hot offer has a short shelf life. If you say no, say no because you have a better plan, not because you expect the offer to wait.__
We were pretty naïve about it.
blocks.who: Mark Zuckerberg on the Synapse offers, 2004

blocks.text: Read this twice. He walked away from a million at 18.
He took a lesson from it. By 2004 he said he kept a lawyer for his products, so he would not be so naive again. He also kept Adam D'Angelo as a close friend.
The email from Harvard
Near the end of his time at Exeter, the Harvard admissions email arrived. Mark later told Harvard's graduates exactly where he was that day.
I was playing Civilization and I ran downstairs, got my dad, and for some reason, his reaction was to video me opening the email.
He got in. "That could have been a really sad video," he joked. He also said that getting into Harvard was still the thing his parents were most proud of him for, even after everything else he did.

blocks.text: Look at the teenage Mark as a whole. He wasn't a lonely genius in a basement. He made movies with his sister, pranked his parents, fenced and read Latin. But one thread ran through all of it. He kept building things, giving them away, and watching how people used them.
Lesson: ship small things often. Synapse got noticed because it was public.

chapters.title: Harvard, a Prank and a Week of Code

blocks.text: Mark arrived at Harvard in the autumn of 2002 as a member of the class of 2006. He studied computer science. Fifteen years later, Harvard's student paper noted that his very first class there was CS 121, a computer science course taught by Harry Lewis, a former dean of the college.
In his second year he lived in Kirkland House, one of Harvard's undergraduate houses. His dorm room there became the most famous dorm room in tech history.

photo.caption: Kirkland House at Harvard. Mark launched thefacebook.com from his dorm room here in February 2004.
photo.author: Bostonian13

blocks.text: Side project one: CourseMatch

At the start of his sophomore year, in the autumn of 2003, he built a site called CourseMatch. Students could choose to share which courses they were taking, so you could see who else was in your classes.
It was a small tool. But it planted an idea: people care a lot about who else is around them. That idea was later folded straight into thefacebook.com.
Small tools teach you what people really want. CourseMatch did.

CourseMatch was not alone. The Crimson later listed other Zuckerberg experiments from this period that never launched: a screensaver that showed your friends' AOL Instant Messenger away messages, and software to keep music in sync across computers. He even dreamed of getting all of Harvard to play the same song at the same moment. He never did it.
Notice the theme. An away message is a tiny public status update. A shared song is a shared moment. Almost every one of these toys was about seeing what other people were doing, right now.
Side project two: Facemash, and the trouble it caused

On a Tuesday night in late October 2003, Mark was bored. At ==8:13 p.m.== he started a new project and wrote about it as he went in an online journal. The idea copied a site called Hot or Not: show two students' photos side by side and let visitors vote on who was more attractive.

To get the photos, he broke into the online student directories, called facebooks, that Harvard's houses kept. He started with Kirkland and went through the houses one by one. Just before 1 a.m. he posted, =="Let the hacking begin."== He called the hacking "child's play." By around 4 a.m. he had the photos, and the site was done just before 7:30 a.m. on Halloween.

He sent the link to a few friends for feedback. It spread to mailing lists, including the Institute of Politics. Traffic more than quadrupled within hours. His computer slowed so badly that it was stuck on its screen saver.

blocks.text: The backlash was fast and fair. Student groups including Fuerza Latina and the Association of Black Harvard Women criticised the site, because students' photos were being used and ranked without their permission. Mark shut it down and emailed apologies to both groups.
I hope you understand, this is not how I meant for things to go, and I apologize for any harm done
blocks.who: Mark Zuckerberg, quoted in the Harvard Crimson, Nov 2003

blocks.text: Harvard's Administrative Board, its main disciplinary body, called him in. It accused him of breaching security, violating copyrights and violating individual privacy. The outcome: he was not forced to withdraw or leave school for any length of time. He would not say whether he got a smaller penalty.

His own words at the time show both sides of him. He said his real interest was "the algorithms and math behind it." He also said, "Issues about violating people's privacy don't seem to be surmountable," and that he was "not willing to risk insulting anyone." __He was brilliant at building, and careless about the people inside what he built. That tension would follow him for twenty years.__
Very important: speed without consent creates enemies. Remember this one.
The going-away party

Facemash had an unexpected side effect. Everyone expected the worst from the Ad Board. As he tells it, his parents came to help him pack, and his friends threw him a going-away party. A student named Priscilla Chan was at that party with a friend.
I'm going to get kicked out in three days, so we need to go on a date quickly.
blocks.who: Mark Zuckerberg, recalling meeting Priscilla Chan, Harvard Commencement 2017

blocks.text: He was not kicked out. Priscilla later became his wife, and he told Harvard's 2017 graduates she was the most important person in his life. He also pushed back on the Hollywood version of these months: the movie, he said, made it seem like Facemash was central to creating Facebook, and it wasn't.
A gap nobody at Harvard was filling

Here is the business gap. In late 2003 Harvard had no single online directory of all its students. Each house kept its own restricted version. The university said it wanted a campus-wide one, but privacy worries had slowed it down, and Facemash had made those worries worse. In December an official admitted, "No staff or technical resources have been assigned yet."

Meanwhile, three seniors, the twins Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss and Divya Narendra, asked Mark to help program their own site for Harvard students, later called ConnectU. He worked on it briefly, then left. Soon after, his own site launched. The three later sued, claiming he stole their idea; Mark denied it and called their claims baseless.

For example of how that dispute ended: the two sides eventually signed a settlement in which the Winklevosses gave up ConnectU in exchange for cash and a piece of Facebook. When they later tried to undo it, a US appeals court refused in April 2011.
One week of code

Early in 2004, Mark sat down to build the directory himself. He wanted something better than a phone book with faces. Students would make profiles, list their classes and interests, and connect with friends. He took inspiration from Friendster, an early social network. Money came from a classmate, Eduardo Saverin, who put in ==$1,000==, enough to keep the servers running for about two months.

He almost didn't launch it. He told the Crimson that if he hadn't launched it that day, he was ready to drop it and move on. Then, on ==4 February 2004==, a Wednesday, he put thefacebook.com live from his Kirkland House room. He was 19.
If I hadn't launched it that day, I was about to just can it and go on to the next thing I was about to do.

That night he went to Noch's, a spot near campus, with his friend KX Jin. He told KX he was excited to connect Harvard, but that one day someone would connect the whole world. It never crossed his mind that the someone might be them. "We were just college kids," he said later.
He was 19, eating pizza, and didn't think he'd be the one.

Within days, more than ==650 students== had signed up, and he expected about 900 by the next morning. He told the Crimson he could build in a week what the university had not managed in years. He added privacy controls so users could choose who saw their profile, and promised he would not sell anyone's email address.
I think it's kind of silly that it would take the University a couple of years to get around to it. I can do it better than they can, and I can do it in a week.

He also explained, in one sentence, why the site would grow on its own: "The nature of the site is that each user's experience improves if they can get their friends to join it." __That is the network effect, described by a 19-year-old five days after launch.__ Every new user made the site more useful for everyone already on it.
For example: by June 2004, four months after launch, thefacebook.com had almost 160,000 members at colleges across the US. His roommate Dustin Moskovitz helped him open it to more schools.
Not a company yet

In those first months Mark kept saying he was not in it for money. A few ads ran on the site, he said, only because "servers don't grow on trees." When the Crimson asked about his ambitions, he gave a very student answer: "My goal is to not have a job." Eight years later, his letter to Facebook's first public investors began: "Facebook was not originally created to be a company."

One odd footnote: the Crimson reported that Mark got a C+ in a Harvard course on artificial intelligence. And TIME reported that one of his AI instructors at Harvard was Andrew "Boz" Bosworth, who later joined Facebook and rose to become one of its top engineering leaders.
A C+ in AI. Grades are not destiny.
The summer that changed the plan

In June 2004 Mark and a few friends rented a summer sublet in Palo Alto, California, near Stanford and the big venture capital firms. The plan was a summer of work on their projects, with school due to start again in the autumn. Silicon Valley had a pull on him. "Palo Alto was kind of like this mythical place where all the techs used to come from," he said.

He never went back to class. Looking back, he said it was "never a formal decision"; the team simply did not return. Harvard's most famous dropout had just begun. And he was honest, years later, about the safety net that made the risk possible.
If I had to support my family growing up instead of having time to code, if I didn't know I'd be fine if Facebook didn't work out, I wouldn't be standing here today.

blocks.text: Put these years together and a clear pattern shows. Mark did not have one lucky idea. He built ZuckNet, games, Synapse, CourseMatch and Facemash before Facebook, and each one taught him something about people and software. The real company, and the real fights, were about to begin.
Six projects before the big one. Keep building.

Most people think Mark Zuckerberg built one thing. He actually built, bought or bet on about twenty. The list includes a music plug-in from high school, a hot-or-not site that got him hauled before a Harvard discipline board, a file-sharing tool, an ad system that told your friends what you bought, a phone launcher with terrible reviews, a solar drone, a digital currency and a personal AI agent.

This chapter goes through them in order. For each one you get the problem, the decision, where the first money came from and how it ended. __Notice how often the flops and the giant wins come from the same habit: building fast, shipping early and buying what he could not build.__
Count the failures. Then count the wins. Both lists are long.

blocks.name: Synapse Media Player
blocks.idea: A plug-in for the popular Winamp music player that learned what you liked to listen to and built matching playlists for you. In plain words, it was a tiny, early version of the "recommended for you" idea that later ran Spotify and YouTube.
blocks.decision: Mark built it with his school friend Adam D'Angelo as an independent project, and they put it online for free instead of selling it. When companies came knocking, the two first said no, then later changed their minds.
blocks.howStarted: Two teenagers, a school project and a free download. A link on the tech site Slashdot brought a wave of attention.
blocks.funding: No outside money at all. It was built with their own time and released free.
blocks.whatHappened: After the Slashdot link, AOL, WinAmp and Microsoft all showed interest. Mark later recalled offers of up to about $1 million, then one of about $2 million. By his own account they decided to accept an offer only after reaching college, and by then the buyer had lost interest. He told The Crimson he had been naive and now kept lawyers for his products.
blocks.lesson: Interest is not an offer, and an offer is not money in the bank. When a real buyer is at the table, decide quickly or be ready to walk away for good.

blocks.name: CourseMatch
blocks.idea: A small website that let Harvard students see who else was taking the same courses, so they could pick classes with friends.
blocks.decision: He built it because the information already existed but nobody had connected it. The idea of linking people through their classes later became one of the first features of thefacebook.
blocks.howStarted: Built alone in his dorm during his sophomore year.
blocks.funding: None. It was a student side project.
blocks.whatHappened: CourseMatch did not become a company. Its core idea was folded into thefacebook.com a few months later, where profiles listed the classes you were taking.
blocks.lesson: Small tools are cheap experiments. Keep the part people loved and move it into your next product.

blocks.name: Facemash
blocks.idea: A copy of the site hotornot.com for Harvard. It showed two students' photos side by side and asked visitors to vote on who was "hotter".
blocks.decision: He built it over the last week of October 2003, pulling ID photos from the online "facebooks" of nine Harvard houses, partly by hacking into house websites. He did not ask anyone's permission.
blocks.howStarted: One student, one laptop, one week. The link spread through campus email lists and traffic quadrupled in a day.
blocks.funding: None.
blocks.whatHappened: By 10 p.m. on its busiest day it had 450 visitors who cast at least 22,000 votes. Student groups, including Fuerza Latina and the Association of Harvard Black Women, criticised it on their email lists. He took it down, and was then called before Harvard's Administrative Board on charges of breaching security, violating copyrights and violating individual privacy. He was allowed to stay at Harvard; he would not say if he got a lesser punishment.
blocks.lesson: Growth that hurts people is not growth. He saw how fast a social site could spread, but he also learned that privacy mistakes follow you.

blocks.text: Issues about violating people's privacy don't seem to be surmountable
blocks.who: Mark Zuckerberg, explaining why he took Facemash down, 2003

blocks.text: The privacy theme starts here, in 2003. It never goes away.

blocks.name: Thefacebook / Facebook / Meta Platforms
blocks.idea: An online directory of Harvard students with profiles, photos, interests, classes and relationship status, so you could look up and connect with people you actually knew. Harvard was planning its own version, and Mark thought it would take the university years.
blocks.decision: The site was built around real people you already knew, not strangers. It grew college by college instead of opening to everyone at once. Early on he resisted venture capital and turned down buyers, including a $1 billion offer from Yahoo in 2006.
blocks.howStarted: He launched it from his room in Kirkland House on 4 February 2004 and said he built it in about a week. More than 650 students signed up within days. By June 2004 it had almost 160,000 members across many colleges, and by that summer a small team had moved into a sublet in Palo Alto, California. The company was incorporated in Delaware in July 2004.
blocks.funding: The first money was tiny: his classmate and co-founder Eduardo Saverin put in $1,000 of start-up money. Ads paid for the servers from the very start. Then came an angel round of about $500,000 from PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel in 2004, and a venture round from Accel Partners in April 2005.
blocks.whatHappened: By September 2005 it had 3.85 million members at 882 colleges. In 2011 it earned $3.71 billion in revenue and $1 billion in profit, with 845 million monthly users. It went public in May 2012 at $38 a share, renamed itself Meta in October 2021, and in 2025 earned $200.97 billion in revenue and $60.46 billion in profit, with 3.58 billion people using its apps every day.
blocks.lesson: Start with a small, dense group that loves the product, then expand. And keep control: he could say no to Yahoo because he still owned the decision.

blocks.text: I can do it better than they can, and I can do it in a week.
blocks.who: Mark Zuckerberg on Harvard's plans for an online facebook, February 2004

blocks.text: He was 19 here. Nineteen.

blocks.name: Wirehog
blocks.idea: A file-sharing program tied to thefacebook. Unlike Kazaa or Napster-style networks, it only let you swap files (photos, music, documents, videos) with people who were already your friends.
blocks.decision: In the summer of 2004 Mark spent much of his time in Palo Alto working on Wirehog, not on thefacebook. He even said his return to Harvard partly depended on how popular Wirehog became. He insisted it was meant for personal files, not for pirating copyrighted material.
blocks.howStarted: Built by Mark, Andrew McCollum and Adam D'Angelo. A test version went out by invitation in October 2004, and it officially launched at Harvard and Stanford in November 2004.
blocks.funding: Paid for out of the same tiny pot as thefacebook. There was no separate funding.
blocks.whatHappened: More than 1,200 students downloaded it on launch day, and about two-thirds of them shared at least one file. But it was harder to use than thefacebook and slower than normal file-sharing tools. We could not find a reliable record of the exact day it was switched off. What is clear is that it never became a business, while thefacebook went national.
blocks.lesson: Watch where your users actually are. He nearly split his attention between two products, and the simpler one won by a mile.

blocks.text: Wirehog is the first time we see a pattern that repeats for twenty years. __Mark often had a second, shinier idea while his main product was still growing.__ The real skill was not having ideas. It was knowing which one to drop.

blocks.name: Facebook Beacon
blocks.idea: An ad system that took what you did on partner shopping and travel websites, such as buying something, and posted it to your Facebook friends. Advertisers would get word-of-mouth marketing at huge scale.
blocks.decision: Facebook launched it as an automatic feature: you had to work to stop it, rather than choose to turn it on. That single design choice caused the whole disaster.
blocks.howStarted: Launched in late 2007 with outside websites as partners.
blocks.funding: Paid for from Facebook's own budget.
blocks.whatHappened: Users were furious that their shopping was being shown to friends without clear permission. Facebook switched it to opt-in and Mark apologised. Beacon was shut down in 2009, and Facebook agreed to pay $9.5 million to settle a class-action lawsuit. In 2011 Mark himself listed Beacon as a high-profile mistake that overshadowed much of the company's good work.
blocks.lesson: If your product shares people's private actions, the default setting must be "off". Ask first, always.

blocks.name: Poke (and the failed bids for Snapchat)
blocks.idea: Snapchat's disappearing photos were exploding among teenagers. Facebook tried two things: buy Snapchat, or copy it.
blocks.decision: Facebook reportedly offered about $1 billion for Snapchat in 2012 and was turned down. It then launched its own disappearing-message app, Poke. In November 2013, The Wall Street Journal reported that Snapchat had turned down a $3 billion all-cash offer from Facebook.
blocks.howStarted: Built inside Facebook as a quick copy.
blocks.funding: Facebook's own money.
blocks.whatHappened: Poke flopped. Snapchat stayed independent. Facebook later found other ways to compete, but this round was a clear loss.
blocks.lesson: Copying a product is not the same as copying why people love it. Teenagers loved Snapchat partly because it was not Facebook.

blocks.name: Instagram (acquisition)
blocks.idea: A photo-sharing app built for phones. Facebook in 2012 was still a website squeezed onto small screens, and Instagram was growing fast on exactly the device Facebook was weakest on.
blocks.decision: Mark chose to buy instead of compete, and promised to keep Instagram running on its own rather than swallow it into Facebook. Regulators later argued this was a plan to remove a rival; a judge rejected that case in 2025.
blocks.howStarted: Instagram was a two-year-old company with 13 staff and about 30 million users when Facebook announced the deal on 9 April 2012.
blocks.funding: Facebook paid with $300 million in cash plus about 23 million of its own shares, a package headlined at about $1 billion.
blocks.whatHappened: Facebook's shares fell hard after its May 2012 stock market debut. Because much of the price was paid in stock, the deal was worth only about $715 million when it was booked in late 2012. Instagram went on to become one of the most valuable apps in the world.
blocks.lesson: Buy the thing that threatens you while it is still small. Paying in your own shares can be cheaper than you think, or much more expensive, depending on where the stock goes.

blocks.text: That's why we're committed to building and growing Instagram independently.
blocks.who: Mark Zuckerberg, announcing the Instagram deal, 9 April 2012

blocks.text: For example: Instagram had 13 employees. At the headline price of about $1 billion, Facebook paid roughly $77 million per employee. At the booked price of $715 million, it was still about $55 million each.

blocks.name: Facebook Home
blocks.idea: A software layer for Android phones that replaced your home screen and lock screen with Facebook posts and photos. It was the closest Facebook came to making its own phone.
blocks.decision: Instead of building hardware, Facebook tried to take over the screen of other companies' phones, starting with a few HTC and Samsung models, including the HTC First.
blocks.howStarted: Unveiled at a press event on 4 April 2013 and released on 12 April 2013, in the US only.
blocks.funding: Facebook's own budget.
blocks.whatHappened: Within hours of launch, it averaged 2.3 out of 5 stars on Google Play. Of 834 reviews, 398, or 47.7%, gave it one star. It was quietly dropped.
blocks.lesson: People do not want one app to take over their whole phone. Earn space; do not grab it.

blocks.text: Two flops in one year. He kept going anyway.

blocks.name: Internet.org and Free Basics
blocks.idea: In 2013 only about 2.7 billion people, just over one-third of the world, were online. Internet.org aimed to connect the other two-thirds. Its best-known product, Free Basics, let mobile users visit a selected set of websites without paying for data.
blocks.decision: Facebook launched Internet.org on 21 August 2013 with Ericsson, MediaTek, Nokia, Opera, Qualcomm and Samsung. In India, it partnered with Reliance Communications, and when regulators questioned Free Basics, it ran a big newspaper and text-message campaign asking people to lobby for it.
blocks.howStarted: A partnership of phone and chip companies, led by Facebook.
blocks.funding: Paid for by Facebook and its partners.
blocks.whatHappened: Critics, including India's "Save the Internet" movement, said Free Basics broke net neutrality, the idea that all websites should be treated equally. On 8 February 2016 the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India banned charging different prices for data depending on the website. That made Free Basics unworkable in India in its existing form. Facebook said it was disappointed.
blocks.lesson: "Free" is not automatically good in the eyes of users or regulators. If you decide which websites poor people can see, expect a fight.

blocks.text: Anything on the Internet cannot be differentially priced
blocks.who: R.S. Sharma, chairman of TRAI, February 2016

blocks.text: Indian readers: this was decided in your country. Remember it.

blocks.name: WhatsApp (acquisition)
blocks.idea: A simple, cheap messaging app that worked on any phone. It had become the main way hundreds of millions of people texted, especially outside the US.
blocks.decision: Mark agreed to pay a huge price for a company with almost no revenue, betting that messaging would become as important as the news feed. WhatsApp's co-founder Jan Koum joined Facebook's board.
blocks.howStarted: When the deal was announced on 19 February 2014, WhatsApp had over 450 million monthly users, 70% of them active on any given day, and was adding more than 1 million new users a day.
blocks.funding: $4 billion in cash, about $12 billion in Facebook shares, and about $3 billion in restricted shares for WhatsApp staff, vesting over four years. That is about $19 billion in total.
blocks.whatHappened: Because Facebook's share price rose before the deal closed on 6 October 2014, the final package was worth about $21.8 billion. By then WhatsApp had more than 500 million users.
blocks.lesson: Price is about what the company will be, not what it earns today. The risk is real: if you are wrong, you have burned billions.

blocks.text: WhatsApp is on a path to connect 1 billion people.

blocks.name: Oculus and Reality Labs (virtual reality and the metaverse)
blocks.idea: Virtual reality headsets that put you inside a computer-made world. Mark saw it as the next big computing platform after the phone, one that Facebook could own instead of renting space on Apple's and Google's phones.
blocks.decision: He bought Oculus in 2014. In October 2021 he went further and renamed the whole company Meta, splitting its accounts into "Family of Apps" (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger) and "Reality Labs" (headsets, glasses and the metaverse).
blocks.howStarted: Announced on 25 March 2014.
blocks.funding: $400 million in cash plus 23.1 million Facebook shares worth about $1.6 billion, and up to $300 million more if Oculus hit certain goals.
blocks.whatHappened: Reality Labs has lost money every single year. Its operating losses were $10.2 billion in 2021, $13.72 billion in 2022, $16.12 billion in 2023, $17.73 billion in 2024 and $19.19 billion in 2025. In the third quarter of 2026 alone it lost $4.13 billion on revenue of just $443 million. In October 2026 Meta said it expected the losses to narrow to about $15 billion the next year as money shifts to AI.
blocks.lesson: Big founders can afford long bets, but even they must check the bill. A dream that loses billions a year needs clear milestones, or it slowly eats the company's patience.

blocks.text: Oculus has the chance to create the most social platform ever, and change the way we work, play and communicate.

items.label: Reality Labs operating losses, 2021–2025 combined (our sum of Meta's annual figures)

blocks.text: Read that first number again. Seventy-seven billion dollars.

blocks.name: Aquila (solar internet drone)
blocks.idea: A huge, light, solar-powered plane that would fly high above the clouds for months and beam internet to remote areas. It was part of the Internet.org mission.
blocks.decision: Facebook chose to design and build the aircraft itself, through a team in Bridgwater, in the UK.
blocks.howStarted: The Bridgwater team designed, built and tested the aircraft and completed two full-scale test flights.
blocks.funding: Facebook's own money.
blocks.whatHappened: On 27 June 2018 Facebook announced it would stop building its own aircraft and close the Bridgwater facility. It said big aerospace companies were now investing in the same technology, so it would work with partners such as Airbus instead.
blocks.lesson: When bigger experts enter your field, it can be smarter to partner than to keep building alone.

blocks.text: we've decided not to design or build our own aircraft any longer.

blocks.name: Chan Zuckerberg Initiative
blocks.idea: A giving and investing organisation set up with his wife, Priscilla Chan. One headline goal is to help cure, prevent or manage all disease by the end of the century.
blocks.decision: In 2015 the couple pledged to give away 99% of their Meta shares over their lifetimes. They chose a company-like structure (an LLC) controlled by Mark rather than a classic charity, which lets it fund research, invest and back causes.
blocks.howStarted: Launched by the couple in 2015.
blocks.funding: Their own Meta shares. Forbes reports they are spending $3 billion on the disease goal.
blocks.whatHappened: By October 2026, Chan Zuckerberg holding entities owned about 315.8 million Meta Class B shares, which carry about 56.1% of the company's votes. Those entities are what signed the written consent that approved Meta's big share restructuring in October 2026.
blocks.lesson: Giving and control can live in the same structure. Read the fine print of any pledge to see who still holds the votes.

blocks.name: Libra / Diem (digital currency)
blocks.idea: A global digital currency run on blockchain technology, plus a wallet called Calibra that would live inside Messenger and WhatsApp. The pitch: let the billions of people without bank accounts save, send and spend money cheaply.
blocks.decision: Facebook announced it on 18 June 2019 with a group of big partner companies and a launch target of 2020. When regulators pushed back, it renamed the wallet Novi (May 2020) and the currency Diem (December 2020).
blocks.howStarted: Run through an independent-looking association of partner companies, with Facebook's new subsidiary Calibra building the wallet.
blocks.funding: Facebook plus partner companies.
blocks.whatHappened: Payments giants ran away fast. PayPal left in early October 2019, and eBay, Mastercard, Stripe, Visa and Mercado Pago followed a week later. In January 2022 the project was wound down and its technology was sold to Silvergate Capital, for a price reported at about $200 million.
blocks.lesson: You cannot launch a new kind of money without the people who regulate money. Win the regulators before you win the headlines.

blocks.name: Jio Platforms stake (India)
blocks.idea: Buy a big minority stake in Reliance's Jio Platforms, whose cheap mobile data brought hundreds of millions of Indians online, and connect it with WhatsApp for shopping and small business.
blocks.decision: Four years after Free Basics was blocked, Facebook came back to India through a partner instead of on its own. The plan was to link Reliance's JioMart with WhatsApp so people could buy from local shops.
blocks.howStarted: Announced on 21 April 2020.
blocks.funding: $5.7 billion (INR 43,574 crore) in cash, making Facebook the largest minority shareholder in Jio Platforms.
blocks.whatHappened: It turned a regulatory loss in India into a deal with the country's most powerful company.
blocks.lesson: If you lose a fight in a market, come back with a local partner who knows the ground.

blocks.text: WhatsApp is so ingrained in Indian life that it has become a commonly used verb across many Indian languages and dialects.
blocks.who: Facebook executives David Fischer and Ajit Mohan, April 2020

blocks.name: Giphy (acquisition, then forced sale)
blocks.idea: Giphy is the GIF search engine used inside many apps. Owning it meant owning a piece of how people express themselves in chats and posts everywhere.
blocks.decision: Meta bought it and then ended Giphy's own advertising services.
blocks.howStarted: Bought by Meta as a running company.
blocks.funding: Paid for from Meta's cash.
blocks.whatHappened: On 18 October 2022 the UK's Competition and Markets Authority ordered Meta to sell Giphy in full. It said Meta could restrict rivals' access to GIFs, noting Meta's sites already took 73% of UK users' time on social media, and that Giphy's ad business could have become a competitor.
blocks.lesson: Once you are huge, even small acquisitions get blocked. Regulators look at what a deal stops from happening.

blocks.name: Threads
blocks.idea: A text-based app for public conversations, a direct rival to Twitter (now X), built by the Instagram team.
blocks.decision: Instead of starting from zero, Threads let people log in with their Instagram account, so it launched with a ready-made audience.
blocks.howStarted: Launched on 5 July 2023, with posts of up to 500 characters plus links, photos and videos.
blocks.funding: Meta's own budget.
blocks.whatHappened: It expanded across Europe in December 2023 and began connecting with other open social networks in 2024.
blocks.lesson: Your existing users are your biggest weapon. Use them to launch the next product.

blocks.name: Llama, Superintelligence Labs and Scale AI
blocks.idea: Build world-class AI models, give many of them away, and use them across Meta's apps, ads and devices.
blocks.decision: In July 2023 Meta released Llama 2 free for research and commercial use, with Microsoft as its preferred partner, arguing that an open approach was right. In June 2025, worried about falling behind Google and OpenAI, Mark paid $14.3 billion for 49% of the data-labelling company Scale AI, valuing it above $29 billion, and hired its 28-year-old CEO Alexandr Wang to lead a new "superintelligence" team.
blocks.howStarted: Started inside Meta's existing AI research groups, then rebuilt around Wang's team in 2025.
blocks.funding: Meta's own cash and, by 2026, borrowed money: Meta sold $25 billion of bonds in May 2026.
blocks.whatHappened: Meta's spending on buildings and computers jumped from $39.23 billion in 2024 to $72.22 billion in 2025, and it expected $135–145 billion in 2026. Meta had not yet released its biggest Llama 4 model, previewed in April 2025, when it made the Scale deal.
blocks.lesson: When you fall behind in a race that matters, buy talent and speed. But know that you are betting the company's cash on it.

blocks.name: Muse (personal AI agent)
blocks.idea: An AI agent that does tasks for you: sending emails, booking travel, shopping, scheduling, and even turning big goals, like starting a business, into step-by-step plans. It can open a browser, fill out forms and negotiate on your behalf.
blocks.decision: Meta launched it only in the US and only for adults 18 and over, running each user's agent on its own secure virtual machine. People can use it in a separate Muse app or inside WhatsApp.
blocks.howStarted: Launched on 8 September 2026.
blocks.funding: Meta's own budget, as part of its AI spending.
blocks.whatHappened: In October 2026 Mark said more than 10 million people in the US and Canada had set up Muse accounts and about 25% of them used it on any given day. He said it needs a lot of computing power and he expects to make it more than ten times cheaper to run the next year.
blocks.lesson: A product people use daily is worth more than a flashy demo. Track daily use, not sign-ups.

blocks.text: Look at the whole list and a pattern jumps out. The things he built from scratch outside his core product (Wirehog, Beacon, Poke, Home, Aquila, Libra) mostly failed. __The things he bought early and left alone, like Instagram and WhatsApp, became giants.__ His real superpower was not invention. It was spotting what would threaten him and acting before others did.
Founders: building is not the only way to win.

In the summer of 2004, thefacebook was famous on campuses and broke. The team had moved into a sublet in Palo Alto and later a five-bedroom house in Los Altos they called "Casa Facebook". Over that summer the site fell roughly $50,000 to $60,000 into debt.

Running it cost about $50,000 a month, including salaries for eight people. Ads paid the bills: student groups could post a local announcement for about $15 a day, and big brands like AT&T Wireless, AOL and Monster.com bought banners. On top of that, the ConnectU lawsuit, filed by Harvard students who said Mark took their idea, was costing about $20,000 a month in legal fees.
I need servers just as much as I need food,
blocks.who: Mark Zuckerberg, The Harvard Crimson, February 2005

blocks.text: Servers before food. That is start-up life.

Here is the surprise. Mark did not want venture capital, which is money from professional investors who buy part of a company hoping it grows. He told The Crimson he would rather the team depended on themselves. The first outside money came from Peter Thiel, the PayPal co-founder. Mark described it as basically a loan with interest and some ownership attached, and TechCrunch reported the angel round at about $500,000.
I would just rather be dependent on ourselves,
blocks.who: Mark Zuckerberg on avoiding venture capital, February 2005

blocks.text: For example: an "angel" is a rich individual who invests early, often before there is any profit. Thiel's deal mixed a loan, which has to be paid back with interest, with a slice of ownership. That way the team got cash without handing a big chunk of control to a venture firm.
The first real round

By April 2005 he changed his mind about venture money. Accel Partners invested in a deal TechCrunch reported at $12.2 million, with a rumoured valuation of around $100 million. Valuation means what the whole company is said to be worth, based on the price investors pay for their slice.

The money bought speed. By September 2005 thefacebook had 3.85 million members at 882 colleges, 32 staff in Palo Alto and 4 in Boston. About 60% of members logged in every day. __Daily use was the number that made investors believe.__

items.label: Accel round, April 2005 (as reported by TechCrunch)

blocks.text: The billion-dollar no

In 2006 Yahoo offered $1 billion in cash. Mark was 22. According to Wired's 2007 account, he gave in under pressure in July and verbally agreed to sell. Then Yahoo's own share price dropped 22% overnight after weak forecasts, and its CEO Terry Semel cut the offer to $800 million.

Mark walked away. Two months later Yahoo came back with the original $1 billion, but by then he had convinced his board and his managers that Yahoo was not a serious partner. __A price cut at the last minute showed him how the buyer would treat his company after the sale.__
Twenty-two years old. One billion dollars. He said no.
On 24 October 2007, Microsoft agreed to invest $240 million at a valuation of $15 billion. In return Microsoft became Facebook's exclusive partner for third-party ads, including outside the US.
For example: $240 million for $15 billion of value means Microsoft bought only about 1.6% of the company. It paid a huge price for a tiny slice, plus the right to sell Facebook's ads.
Going public

An IPO, or initial public offering, is when a private company first sells shares on a stock exchange so anyone can buy them. Facebook filed its papers in February 2012. They showed $3.71 billion of revenue and $1 billion of profit in 2011, 845 million monthly users, 3,200 full-time staff, and one surprise: the game company Zynga alone made up about 12% of Facebook's revenue.
Simply put: we don't build services to make money; we make money to build better services.
blocks.who: Mark Zuckerberg, letter to investors in the IPO filing, 2012

blocks.text: On 17 May 2012 Facebook priced its shares at $38 and sold 421.2 million of them, 180 million by the company and the rest by existing holders. That is about $16 billion at the offer price. Trading on Nasdaq was delayed by a technical problem the next day, and the shares closed at just $38.23. Bankers had to buy stock to stop it falling below $38.

On IPO day Mark sold 30.2 million shares at $37.58 each, about $1.1 billion, and kept 503.6 million. Then the price kept sliding. By the time the Instagram deal was booked months later, the shares had fallen so far that the "$1 billion" purchase was worth $715 million.

blocks.text: Facebook's near-death moments were mostly not about cash. They were moments when users, regulators or investors turned against it all at once. Each time, the company survived because Mark changed course, sometimes after a costly delay.
Lawsuits from the start

The ConnectU case followed Facebook for years. In 2008 the parties agreed a settlement valued at $65 million in cash and Facebook stock. The Winklevoss twins later argued they had been misled about the value of the shares and tried to undo it. On 11 April 2011 a US appeals court said no, and the deal stood.
At some point, litigation must come to an end.
blocks.who: Chief Judge Alex Kozinski, US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, 2011

blocks.text: An idea dispute from 2004 was still in court in 2011.
The privacy bill keeps growing

After Beacon, the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC), the government body that protects consumers, reached a privacy agreement with Facebook in November 2011. Facebook promised privacy reviews when building products and independent privacy audits every two years. In his own post that day Mark admitted the company had made "a bunch of mistakes".

Those promises came back to bite. A later settlement with the FTC required Facebook to pay a $5 billion penalty, according to Meta's own filings. __Small privacy shortcuts early on turned into the biggest fines in the company's history.__
2022: the year everything went wrong

In October 2021 Mark renamed Facebook as Meta and bet the company's future on the metaverse. That year the core business was booming, with $117.9 billion in revenue and $39.4 billion of profit. But Reality Labs already lost $10.2 billion.

Then 2022 hit. Revenue fell 1%, to $116.61 billion, a rare yearly drop for a company used to fast growth. Profit fell 41% to $23.2 billion, while Reality Labs lost $13.72 billion. Meanwhile headcount had grown to 86,482 people.
On 9 November 2022 Mark laid off more than 11,000 employees, about 13% of the company. He said he had expected the pandemic boom in online shopping to last, invested for it, and been wrong.
I got this wrong, and I take responsibility for that.
blocks.who: Mark Zuckerberg to Meta employees, 9 November 2022

blocks.text: Read this twice. Founders who say this out loud recover faster.

In March 2023 he went further. In what he called the "Year of Efficiency", Meta cut about 10,000 more jobs and closed about 5,000 open roles. He removed layers of management, asked many managers to go back to hands-on work, and set a rough cap of about 10 direct reports per manager under the principle "flatter is faster".
For example: Meta had 86,482 staff at the end of 2022 and 67,317 at the end of 2023, a 22% drop. Yet 2023 revenue rose 16% to $134.9 billion and profit came back to $39.1 billion.

The comeback was fast. In February 2024 Meta announced its first-ever dividend, a cash payment to shareholders of $0.50 per share every quarter, and added $50 billion to its plan to buy back its own shares. In 2024 profit jumped 59% to $62.36 billion. __Cutting costs did not kill the company. It gave investors their faith back.__

blocks.text: By 2025 Meta was earning money at a scale few companies ever reach: $200.97 billion of revenue and $60.46 billion of profit, with 3.58 billion people using its apps every day. Mark took that money and threw it at artificial intelligence.

In 2025 Meta spent $72.22 billion on data centres, chips and other equipment. For 2026 it planned $135 billion to $145 billion. In the first nine months of 2026 it had already spent $83.06 billion, and in May 2026 it borrowed $25 billion by selling bonds.
For example: the top of that range, $145 billion, equals roughly 72% of all the revenue Meta earned in 2025. Imagine a family spending almost three-quarters of a year's income on one new house.
Founders: this is what betting the company looks like.

The bet came with job cuts. Meta reportedly cut about 8,000 jobs, around 10% of staff, starting in May 2026, to help pay for computing. By 30 September 2026 it had 66,775 employees, 15% fewer than a year before.
The court cases

On 18 November 2025, Judge James Boasberg ruled that the FTC had not shown Meta holds a monopoly today, so Meta did not have to sell Instagram or WhatsApp. The judge said apps like TikTok and YouTube now compete for the same time. The FTC filed an appeal on 20 January 2026.

The child-safety cases went the other way. On 24 March 2026 a New Mexico jury ordered Meta to pay a $375 million civil penalty, and a day later a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube liable in a social media addiction case brought by a 20-year-old woman. In August 2026 Meta agreed a deal with 52 attorneys general for payments of up to about $18.59 billion, about $12.7 billion of it over 10 years and about $5.3 billion that depends on other companies adopting similar teen protections.

On 21 October 2026, a New Mexico judge ordered a $25 billion civil penalty after a jury found Meta had broken the state's Unfair Practices Act more than 43 million times with misleading statements about data and safety. Meta says it will appeal, so this is not final. __The legal bill from the 2010s is now arriving in the 2020s, all at once.__

blocks.text: How the fortune actually works

Mark's wealth is almost all Meta stock. As of 1 October 2026 he owned 1,220,703 Class A shares and 341,215,148 Class B shares. That is about 13.4% of the company's value but 60.6% of the votes, because each Class B share carries ten votes. This is called a dual-class structure, and it means nobody can outvote him.

For example: 342.4 million shares times Meta's closing price of $612.49 on 28 October 2026 comes to about $210 billion. Forbes put his net worth at $210.5 billion on 29 October 2026, sixth in the world.
That makes his fortune swing wildly. Meta closed at $697.52 on 21 October 2026 and at $648.85 the next day. On his shares, that is a paper drop of about $16.7 billion in a single trading day.
Sixteen billion in one day, and nothing he owned changed.
The control move

In October 2026 Meta announced a new type of share, Class C, with no votes at all. Every holder will get one Class C share for each Class A or B share they own, once the change takes effect on 19 January 2027. Meta says this lets it raise money, make acquisitions and pay staff in stock without weakening Mark's majority vote.

Shareholders did not vote on it. The Chan Zuckerberg holding entities, which control about 56.1% of the votes, approved it in writing on 20 October 2026. The filing says a special board committee first proposed a "sunset", a date when his extra voting power would end, and Mark would not accept it. It also says 20% of his new Class C shares can be sold freely, partly so he can pay a possible tax under California's Proposition 40 if voters pass it on 3 November 2026.
there are no time-based or other sunset provisions, thereby allowing Mr. Zuckerberg to maintain generational control.

blocks.text: __This is the thread that ties his whole career together.__ He turned down Yahoo in 2006 because he could. He bought Instagram and WhatsApp because he could. He spent about $77 billion on the metaverse because no one could outvote him. In 2026 he made sure that would stay true for good.

blocks.text: Most mornings Mark Zuckerberg wakes between ==7:00 and 7:30 a.m.==, usually because one of his three daughters has woken him. He reaches for his phone straight away, and he says the news on it is mostly bad. Then he does something few chief executives do. He goes and fights.
I compose myself and go fight for two hours, recenter myself, and it's like, now I can go deal with this stuff.
blocks.who: Mark Zuckerberg, on Theo Von's podcast, 2025

blocks.text: It started as a way to quiet his head. He told Joe Rogan he used to run, "but the problem with running is you can think a lot." So he moved to jiu-jitsu and mixed martial arts, where a wandering mind gets you choked. He also told Rogan why the phone hurts so much first thing: "People reserve the good stuff to tell me in person."
Find the one hour when your brain cannot check the phone.

The rest of the day has been described in pieces over the years. In a 2023 profile he aimed for eight hours of sleep and said "I don't stay up super late at night." Priscilla Chan has said he tucks the children in unless he is travelling or has a board meeting. He told Lex Fridman he goes through what matters most in life with his daughters: health, friends, family and something to look forward to.
Clearing out the small decisions

In November 2014, at Facebook's first public town hall, someone asked why he wore the same gray T-shirt every day. His answer became one of the most copied habits in the startup world. Quartz pointed out the idea behind it, which psychologists call decision fatigue: even small choices, like breakfast or clothes, use up energy.
I really want to clear my life to make it so that I have to make as few decisions as possible about anything except how to best serve the community.
blocks.who: Mark Zuckerberg, Facebook town hall, November 2014

blocks.text: The "small group"

Meta has tens of thousands of staff, but Mark directly oversees only ==25 to 30 people==. He calls them the "small group", and he knows the name is a joke. He described them to Stripe's John Collison in May 2025 as a "core army that can go get anything done across the company". He spends real time making sure they are connected to each other and all know what is going on.

Here is the surprising part. He has no recurring one-on-one meetings with any of them. He does keep only two standing weekly meetings with the group: an open-ended strategy talk and an operating review of company priorities. __The rest of his calendar stays loose on purpose, so he can jump on whatever matters that day.__
I think if you're going to report to me, you need to be able to manage yourself.

He was careful about how far this goes. "I talk to all these people constantly, more than they want to talk to me, I'm sure," he said. He also said that for the rest of the company, management is important and is how people grow. So this rule is for one room, not the whole building.
No one-on-ones only works if every person can manage themselves.
